**Equal bits at position 3 → button 1; different bits → button 2.** The examples do not settle this. A pattern across the Z components favours it.

## Fitting the Y components
- **Y4 = bit 3.** In X2-Y4-Z2 and X6-Y4-Z3, bits 1, 2 and 4 each produce contradictions. Only bit 3 gives a consistent symmetric rule.
- **Y2 = bit 1.** In X1-Y2-Z2, button 3 appears exactly when both bit-1 values are 0.
- **Y1 = bit 4.** In X1-Y1-Z4 and both X3-Y1 tasks, only bit 4 is consistent.

## Fitting the X and Z components
Two assignment families fit X1, X2, X3, Z2 and Z4:

| | X1 | X2 | X3 | Z2 (true/false) | Z4 (true/false) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | at least one | neither | not both | 1 / 3 | 2 / 1 |
| **B** | neither | at least one | both | 3 / 1 | 1 / 2 |

X6-Y4-Z3 on bit 3 fits only two readings:
- X6 = "same", with Z3 true → 2 and false → 3.
- X6 = "exactly one", with Z3 true → 3 and false → 2.

Neither reading appears in any other task, so both stay open.

## The four assignments for X6-Y4-Z4

| Assignment | Equal bits | Different bits |
|---|---|---|
| A + same | 2 | 1 |
| A + exactly one | 1 | 2 |
| B + same | 1 | 2 |
| B + exactly one | 2 | 1 |

The examples allow two opposite answers, so the task is **not determined**.

## Cross-component pattern
In **A + exactly one** and **B + same**, the three Z components use three different "true" buttons and three different "false" buttons. They form a clean permutation over buttons 1–3. The other two assignments repeat buttons: A + same reuses 2 as the "true" button, and B + exactly one reuses 3. The structured pair gives the same answer, so I choose: equal bits at position 3 → **1**, different bits → **2**.

## Predictions (bit 3 of each stimulus)
| # | Input | Bit 3 | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0111 0110 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1100 0101 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 3 | 1100 0011 | 0, 1 | 2 |
| 4 | 0001 0011 | 0, 1 | 2 |
| 5 | 0111 1111 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1110 0010 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 7 | 1110 1100 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 8 | 1001 1000 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 9 | 1111 1010 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 10 | 0010 1101 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 11 | 0101 0001 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 12 | 0110 1011 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 13 | 1000 1101 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 14 | 1000 0110 | 0, 1 | 2 |
| 15 | 1110 0100 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 16 | 1011 0110 | 1, 1 | 1 |

The other reading would swap every 1 and 2. My confidence of 0.62 reflects a modest lean from the pattern.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
